o: The anterior limb lies between the head of the caudate nucleus and the lentiform nucleus
The anterior limb separates the caudate head medially from the lentiform nucleus laterally. The posterior limb lies between thalamus and lentiform nucleus.
Corticobulbar (corticonuclear) fibres occupy the genu
Corticonuclear fibres to the motor cranial nerve nuclei lie in the genu.
In the posterior limb, corticospinal fibres for the lower limb lie anterior to those for the upper limb
In the posterior limb the arrangement runs face/arm (anterior) to leg (posterior).
The optic radiation passes through the retrolentiform part
The optic radiation (geniculocalcarine) passes in the retrolentiform part. The auditory radiation passes in the sublentiform part.

questions.s: Arteries supplying the internal capsule include the:
o: Lateral striate (lenticulostriate) branches of the middle cerebral artery
These supply most of the upper parts of both limbs. Their rupture is the classic cause of capsular haemorrhage.
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
AICA supplies the lower pons, the inferolateral cerebellum and usually gives the labyrinthine artery. It does not reach the capsule.
Superior cerebellar artery
It supplies the upper surface of the cerebellum and parts of the midbrain, not the internal capsule.
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
PICA supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum, not the capsule.
The ventral posteromedial nucleus receives the trigeminal lemniscus and taste fibres
VPM relays sensation from the face (trigeminothalamic fibres) and taste (from the solitary nucleus) to the postcentral gyrus and insula.
The ventral lateral nucleus receives fibres from the dentate nucleus of the contralateral cerebellum
Dentatothalamic fibres cross in the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation and relay in VL to the motor cortex.
The anterior nucleus receives the mammillothalamic tract
The anterior nucleus is part of the Papez circuit and projects to the cingulate gyrus.
The reticular nucleus projects mainly to the cerebral cortex
The reticular nucleus lies outside the external medullary lamina. Its GABAergic neurones project back to other thalamic nuclei, not to the cortex.
Receives fibres from the temporal retina of the ipsilateral eye
Uncrossed temporal fibres reach the ipsilateral LGB.
Relays auditory impulses to the transverse temporal gyri
That is the medial geniculate body.
Has six layers, with crossed fibres ending in layers 1, 4 and 6
Contralateral (crossed nasal) fibres end in layers 1, 4 and 6. Ipsilateral fibres end in 2, 3 and 5.
Projects to the superior colliculus through the brachium of the superior colliculus
Fibres from the optic tract bypass the LGB to reach the superior colliculus and pretectum through the superior brachium. The LGB projects to the calcarine cortex.
The lentiform nucleus consists of the putamen and globus pallidus
The lentiform (lenticular) nucleus is the putamen laterally plus the globus pallidus medially.
The corpus striatum includes the caudate nucleus and the lentiform nucleus
Corpus striatum = caudate + lentiform. The striatum (neostriatum) = caudate + putamen.
The claustrum lies between the external capsule and the extreme capsule
The claustrum is a thin sheet of grey matter between the external capsule (medially) and extreme capsule (laterally), deep to the insula.
The tail of the caudate nucleus lies in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle
The tail of the caudate lies in the roof of the inferior horn. The hippocampus forms the floor.
The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries olivocerebellar fibres
Olivocerebellar (climbing) fibres from the contralateral inferior olive enter through the inferior peduncle.
The middle cerebellar peduncle carries only afferent pontocerebellar fibres
The middle peduncle is composed of crossed pontocerebellar fibres from the pontine nuclei.
The superior cerebellar peduncle carries the dorsal spinocerebellar tract
The dorsal spinocerebellar tract enters through the inferior peduncle. The ventral spinocerebellar tract enters through the superior peduncle.
Efferent fibres from the dentate nucleus decussate in the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus
The decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles is in the caudal midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculi.

questions.s: Concerning the cerebellar cortex and nuclei:
o: Granule cells are the only output neurones of the cerebellar cortex
Purkinje cell axons are the sole output of the cortex. Granule cell axons form the parallel fibres within the cortex.
Purkinje cells are inhibitory (GABAergic)
Purkinje cells inhibit the deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei.
The deep nuclei from medial to lateral are dentate, emboliform, globose and fastigial
From medial to lateral the order is fastigial, globose, emboliform, dentate. The dentate is the most lateral.
Mossy fibres synapse with granule cells in the cerebellar glomeruli
Mossy fibres (pontocerebellar, spinocerebellar, vestibular and others) end on granule cell dendrites in the glomeruli. Climbing fibres from the inferior olive end on Purkinje cells.
Is separated from the body of the cerebellum by the posterolateral fissure
The posterolateral fissure is the first fissure to appear and separates the flocculonodular lobe.
Is phylogenetically the oldest part (archicerebellum)
It is the vestibulocerebellum.
Has major connections with the vestibular nuclei
It receives primary and secondary vestibular fibres and projects to the vestibular nuclei, directly and through the fastigial nucleus.
Is separated from the anterior lobe by the primary fissure
The primary fissure separates the anterior lobe from the posterior (middle) lobe.
It is present in the body and inferior horn of the lateral ventricle
The plexus runs along the choroid fissure from the interventricular foramen through the body, atrium (glomus) and inferior horn.
It is present in the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle
There is no choroid plexus in the anterior (frontal) or posterior (occipital) horns.
It is present in the roof of the third ventricle
Two strands hang from the tela choroidea in the roof of the third ventricle.
It is present in the cerebral aqueduct
The aqueduct contains no choroid plexus.
Has the facial colliculus in the floor of its medullary part
The facial colliculus is in the pontine part of the floor. The hypoglossal and vagal trigones are in the medullary part.
Communicates with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture
The foramen of Magendie in the lower roof opens into the cerebellomedullary cistern.
Communicates directly with the third ventricle through the interventricular foramina
It communicates with the third ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct. The interventricular foramina join the lateral and third ventricles.
Communicates with the pontine cistern through the lateral apertures
Last's: the lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) open just behind VIII into the pontine cistern.
The interventricular foramina lie between the fornix and the anterior pole of the thalamus
Last's: the anterior columns of the fornix form the anterior margins of the interventricular foramina, with the anterior pole of the thalamus behind.
The optic and infundibular recesses lie in its anterior inferior wall
The optic recess lies above the chiasma, the infundibular recess in the stalk.
Its lateral walls are formed entirely by the thalamus
The upper lateral wall is thalamus. Below the hypothalamic sulcus it is hypothalamus.
The pineal recess lies in its posterior wall
The posterior wall has the suprapineal and pineal recesses, with the posterior commissure below and the habenular commissure above the pineal stalk.
The supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei produce vasopressin and oxytocin
Their magnocellular neurones produce ADH and oxytocin, transported down the hypothalamohypophysial tract to the posterior pituitary.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives direct retinal input
The retinohypothalamic tract to the suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates circadian rhythms.
The fornix ends mainly in the mammillary body
Most postcommissural fornix fibres end in the mammillary body.
Releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary via the hypothalamohypophysial nerve tract
Releasing hormones from the arcuate (infundibular) and other nuclei reach the anterior lobe via the hypophysial portal veins, not by axons.

questions.s: Concerning functional areas of the cerebral cortex:
o: The primary auditory cortex is in the transverse temporal gyri
Heschl's gyri (areas 41 and 42) on the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus.
The motor speech area of Broca lies in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
The pars opercularis and triangularis (areas 44 and 45).
The frontal eye field lies in the precentral gyrus
The frontal eye field (area 8) lies in the posterior part of the middle frontal gyrus, in front of the precentral gyrus.
The primary visual cortex lies on the walls of the calcarine sulcus
Area 17, marked by the stria of Gennari.
The anterior commissure interconnects the temporal lobes and olfactory structures
It crosses in the lamina terminalis, linking olfactory regions and the middle and inferior temporal gyri.
The forceps minor passes through the splenium of the corpus callosum
The forceps minor passes through the genu to the frontal lobes. The forceps major passes through the splenium to the occipital lobes.
The posterior commissure carries fibres concerned with the consensual light reflex
Pretectal fibres to the contralateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus cross in the posterior commissure.
The anterior commissure crosses in the posterior wall of the third ventricle
The anterior commissure crosses in the lamina terminalis, in the anterior wall. The posterior and habenular commissures are in the posterior wall.

questions.s: Concerning the arteries at the base of the brain:
o: The oculomotor nerve passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
The nerve emerges between these two arteries close to the basilar bifurcation.
The anterior cerebral artery passes above the optic nerve
The A1 segment runs forward and medially above the optic nerve or chiasma to the longitudinal fissure.
The recurrent artery of Heubner usually arises from the middle cerebral artery

Heubner's artery arises from the anterior cerebral artery. Last's describes it as the largest medial striate branch, supplying the more posterior part of the capsule including the leg area (absent in 3%). Many neurosurgical texts emphasise the head of caudate and anterior limb, so know both.
The posterior communicating artery is closely related to the oculomotor nerve
The oculomotor nerve runs alongside the posterior communicating artery. An aneurysm at its origin compresses the nerve, and the pupil is often affected first.
Arises from the internal carotid artery
Last's: it arises from the termination of the ICA or its near neighbours (MCA or posterior communicating). It is the fourth artery to the cerebrum and does not supply cortex.
Supplies the choroid plexus of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle
It enters the choroid fissure to supply the inferior horn plexus.
Supplies the optic tract and lateral geniculate body

Last's: it supplies the optic chiasma and tract, lateral geniculate body, choroid plexus (entering the choroid fissure at the tip of the inferior horn) and the posterior part of the internal capsule. Occlusion gives contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia.
Supplies the head of the caudate nucleus
The head of the caudate is supplied mainly by the recurrent artery of Heubner and lateral striate arteries. The anterior choroidal supplies hippocampus, amygdala, posterior limb, optic tract and LGB.

questions.s: Occlusion of the cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery (beyond the origin of its striate branches) would be expected to produce:
o: Contralateral hemiplegia affecting the face and arm more than the leg

Cortical MCA territory includes the face and arm motor areas. The leg area is on the medial surface (ACA). Last's notes that occlusion of the stem, including the striate arteries, gives complete contralateral hemiplegia.
Contralateral sensory loss over the face and arm
The face and arm areas of the postcentral gyrus lie on the lateral surface in MCA territory.
Aphasia if the dominant hemisphere is affected
Broca's and Wernicke's areas are both in MCA territory.
Contralateral loss of sensation in the leg predominating
Leg sensory cortex is on the medial surface (paracentral lobule), supplied by the ACA.
The great cerebral vein is formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins
They unite beneath the splenium to form the great cerebral vein (of Galen).
The internal cerebral vein is formed at the interventricular foramen by the thalamostriate and choroidal veins
The thalamostriate and choroidal veins (with septal veins) unite behind the column of the fornix.
The superior anastomotic vein connects the superficial middle cerebral vein with the transverse sinus
The superior anastomotic vein (Trolard) drains to the superior sagittal sinus. The inferior anastomotic vein (Labbe) drains to the transverse sinus.
Cerebral veins have no valves
The cerebral veins and dural sinuses are valveless.
In the adult it usually ends at the level of the L1/L2 intervertebral disc
The conus medullaris usually ends at L1/2. At birth it ends at L3.
The denticulate ligaments are attached between the anterior and posterior nerve roots
The pia mater forms about 21 pairs of denticulate ligaments, attached to the dura between the roots.
The filum terminale is attached to the back of the first coccygeal segment
The filum pierces the dural sac at S2 and attaches to the dorsum of the coccyx.
The lateral grey horn is present from C1 to C8
Last's: a lateral horn of preganglionic sympathetic cells is present from T1 to L2, and a similar small lateral horn of parasympathetic cells lies in S2 to S4.

questions.s: Concerning the ascending tracts of the spinal cord:
o: The fasciculus cuneatus is present only above about the T6 segment
The fasciculus cuneatus carries upper limb and upper trunk fibres, entering above about T6.
In the posterior columns, sacral fibres lie most medially
Fibres are added laterally as they ascend, so sacral fibres lie most medially in the fasciculus gracilis.
Spinothalamic fibres cross in the posterior white commissure

They cross in front of the central canal (anterior white commissure). Last's: crossing is transverse in the lowest cord but increasingly oblique higher up, taking 4 to 5 segments in the cervical region.
The dorsal spinocerebellar tract arises from the nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's column)

Last's: the thoracic nucleus (Clarke's column, lamina VII) occupies all the thoracic and first two lumbar segments (T1 to L2). Cervical proprioception reaches the cerebellum by the accessory cuneate nucleus and cuneocerebellar tract instead.

questions.s: A hemisection of the spinal cord at T10 (Brown-Sequard) would produce below the lesion:
o: Ipsilateral upper motor neurone paralysis
The lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla.
Contralateral loss of proprioception
The dorsal columns are uncrossed in the cord, so proprioception and vibration loss are ipsilateral.
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion
Pain and temperature loss is contralateral, because the anterolateral tract has already crossed.
Bilateral complete loss of light touch
Light touch is partly carried in both dorsal columns and anterior spinothalamic tracts, so it is usually relatively preserved.
About 85 percent of corticospinal fibres decussate in the lower medulla
Most fibres cross in the pyramidal decussation. The rest descend uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract.
Fibres for the lower limb lie most laterally in the tract
In the lateral corticospinal tract, cervical fibres are medial and sacral fibres lateral.
It lies anterior to the lateral spinothalamic tract
The lateral corticospinal tract lies in the posterior part of the lateral funiculus, in front of the posterior horn. The spinothalamic tract lies anterolaterally.
Many fibres arise from cells in the postcentral gyrus
Only about a third of corticospinal fibres arise from area 4. Others come from premotor and parietal cortex, including the postcentral gyrus.

questions.s: Concerning the blood supply of the spinal cord:
o: The anterior spinal artery is formed by branches of both vertebral arteries
A branch from each vertebral artery unites in front of the medulla to form the single anterior spinal artery.
The anterior spinal artery supplies about the anterior two-thirds of the cord

Last's: it supplies the whole cord anterior to the posterior grey columns. Anterior spinal artery syndrome spares the posterior columns, and pial vessels may spare the superficial sacral fibres (sacral sparing).
The arteria radicularis magna (of Adamkiewicz) usually enters on the right side
Last's: it is slightly commoner on the left and at T10 or T11, but may be anywhere from T7 to L4, so it cannot be relied on to accompany a low thoracic root.
The posterior spinal arteries usually arise from the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries or vertebral arteries

Last's: each arises from PICA or the vertebral artery at the foramen magnum, is usually double, and runs through and behind the posterior rootlets. Each supplies the posterior grey and white columns of its own side.

questions.s: The lateral medullary syndrome (PICA or vertebral artery occlusion) typically includes:
o: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the face
Facial loss is ipsilateral, because the spinal tract and nucleus of V are uncrossed. Body loss is contralateral, from the crossed spinothalamic tract.
Ipsilateral paralysis of the tongue
The hypoglossal nucleus and nerve are medial. Tongue paralysis belongs to the medial medullary syndrome.
Contralateral hemiplegia
The pyramid is medial (anterior spinal artery territory), so hemiplegia is not a feature.
Ipsilateral paralysis of the palate, pharynx and vocal cord
Involvement of the nucleus ambiguus causes dysphagia and dysphonia. Ipsilateral Horner's, vertigo, nystagmus and ataxia also occur.
The tongue deviates towards the side of the lesion on protrusion
Ipsilateral hypoglossal paralysis: the intact genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the paralysed side.
There is contralateral hemiplegia
The pyramid is involved above the decussation.
There is contralateral loss of touch and proprioception
The medial lemniscus is involved after it has crossed.
There is ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature on the face
That is a feature of the lateral medullary syndrome (spinal tract of V).

questions.s: Regarding the superficial attachments of the cranial nerves to the brainstem:
o: The hypoglossal nerve emerges between the pyramid and the olive
Its rootlets emerge in the preolivary (anterolateral) sulcus.
The abducent nerve emerges at the junction of the pons and pyramid
It emerges at the lower border of the pons, above the pyramid.
The trochlear nerve emerges from the ventral surface of the midbrain
The trochlear is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal surface, just below the inferior colliculus. It then crosses in the superior medullary velum.
The glossopharyngeal, vagus and cranial accessory nerves emerge posterior to the olive
They emerge in the postolivary sulcus, between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.s: Concerning features of the floor of the fourth ventricle:
o: The facial colliculus overlies the abducent nucleus
The colliculus is formed by facial motor fibres looping (internal genu) around the abducent nucleus.
The area postrema lies outside the blood-brain barrier
It is a circumventricular organ concerned with vomiting.
The vagal trigone overlies the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
The hypoglossal trigone lies medially, the vagal trigone laterally.
The striae medullares cross the floor at the level of the pontomedullary junction

Last's: the medullary striae cross the floor at its widest part, between the pontine and medullary parts. They are aberrant fibres from pontine nuclei passing to the cerebellum by the inferior peduncle.

questions.s: At the level of the superior colliculus, the midbrain contains the:
o: Oculomotor nucleus
The oculomotor complex lies in front of the aqueduct at this level.
Red nucleus
The red nucleus lies in the tegmentum at the superior colliculus level and is traversed by the oculomotor fibres.
Trochlear nucleus
The trochlear nucleus is at the level of the inferior colliculus.
Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles
This is at the level of the inferior colliculus.
A lesion of the optic chiasma typically causes bitemporal hemianopia
Crossing nasal fibres serve the temporal fields.
Fibres of Meyer's loop serving the contralateral upper quadrant pass through the temporal lobe
Inferior retinal fibres loop around the inferior horn. A temporal lesion produces a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
The pupillary light reflex is relayed through the lateral geniculate body
Light reflex fibres leave the optic tract before the LGB to reach the pretectal nuclei.
A lesion of the optic tract produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia
Each tract carries fibres from the ipsilateral temporal and contralateral nasal retina.
The amygdala lies in the temporal lobe in front of the tip of the inferior horn
The amygdaloid body lies deep to the uncus, anterior to the inferior horn tip.
The stria terminalis runs from the amygdala alongside the thalamostriate vein
The stria terminalis runs in the groove between caudate and thalamus with the thalamostriate vein, to the septal area and hypothalamus.
The hippocampus forms the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle
It forms the floor (medial part) of the inferior horn.
The mammillothalamic tract projects to the medial dorsal nucleus of the thalamus
It projects to the anterior thalamic nucleus.
The pontine cistern contains the vertebral arteries
Last's: the pontine cistern contains the basilar artery and nerves V to XII. The vertebral arteries and PICA lie in the lateral part of the cisterna magna.
The interpeduncular cistern contains the anterior communicating artery
The anterior communicating artery lies in the chiasmatic cistern. The interpeduncular cistern holds the posterior circle, the pituitary stalk and nerves III and IV.
The cisterna magna receives CSF from the lateral apertures
It receives CSF from the median aperture. The lateral apertures open into the pontine cistern.
The cerebellomedullary cistern can be entered by a needle passed through the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane
Cisternal puncture, in the midline, through the membrane and spinal dura.
The mesencephalic nucleus contains the cell bodies of primary proprioceptive neurones
Unusually, these are primary sensory neurones lying within the CNS, carrying proprioception from the muscles of mastication and periodontal ligaments.
The spinal nucleus extends down into the upper cervical cord
It extends to about C2 or C3, continuous with the substantia gelatinosa.
Pain and temperature from the face relay in the principal (chief) sensory nucleus
Pain and temperature relay in the spinal nucleus (pars caudalis). The principal nucleus serves discriminative touch.
The motor nucleus lies in the pons medial to the principal sensory nucleus
The motor nucleus lies medial to the principal sensory nucleus in the mid pons.

questions.s: The nucleus ambiguus supplies motor fibres to the:
o: Stylopharyngeus via the glossopharyngeal nerve
The cranial-most part of the nucleus ambiguus supplies stylopharyngeus via IX.
Intrinsic muscles of the larynx via the vagus
The intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied via the recurrent and external laryngeal nerves.
Muscles of the soft palate except tensor veli palatini
Via the pharyngeal plexus (vagus and cranial accessory).
Striated muscle of the upper oesophagus via the vagus
Last's: the upper part of the nucleus serves the palate, the middle part the pharynx and oesophagus, the lowest part the larynx.

questions.s: The nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives:
o: Taste fibres from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the facial nerve
Taste via chorda tympani, cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion.
Taste fibres from the posterior third of the tongue via the glossopharyngeal nerve
Cell bodies in the inferior ganglion of IX.
Visceral afferents from the carotid sinus via the glossopharyngeal nerve
Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input via the carotid sinus nerve.
Visceral afferents from the thoracic and abdominal viscera via the vagus
General visceral afferents from the vagus end in the caudal part of the nucleus.
In the central nervous system, myelin is formed by oligodendrocytes
One oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of many axons.
In peripheral nerves, myelin is formed by satellite cells
Peripheral myelin is formed by Schwann cells (neurolemmocytes). Satellite cells surround neurones in ganglia.
The corticospinal tracts are fully myelinated at birth
Corticospinal tracts are not fully myelinated at birth. Myelination continues during the first two years, which explains the extensor plantar response in infancy.
Microglia are the phagocytic cells of the CNS
Microglia are of mesodermal (monocyte) origin and act as CNS macrophages.
The pineal gland frequently calcifies in adults
Last's: corpora amylacea calcify, and after about 40 years they normally cast a shadow on skull radiographs. A displaced pineal indicates a supratentorial mass.
The habenular nuclei receive fibres through the stria medullaris thalami
The stria medullaris thalami carries fibres from the septal area to the habenula.
The habenulointerpeduncular tract (fasciculus retroflexus) projects to the interpeduncular nucleus
It projects from the habenula to the interpeduncular nucleus of the midbrain.
The pineal gland lies above the posterior commissure and below the splenium
The pineal lies in the posterior wall of the third ventricle, below the splenium, with the posterior commissure in its lower lamina.
